·
第4️⃣ 天：从满洲里往呼伦湖解锁美丽的风车秋色，在呼伦湖荡秋千欣赏静谧的湖水，沿途前行抵达186彩带河，登高俯瞰蜿蜒曲折的额尔古纳河，傍晚抵达黑山头，赴一场草原绝美日落，晚餐吃当地特色的烧烤
·
第5️⃣天：从黑山头前往恩和俄式的童话乡村，彩色木刻楞小屋搭配秋日田园，满满的异域田园风情，午后打卡整片金黄白桦林秋风落叶氛围感拉满，一路游玩抵达额尔古纳休息，领队带我们去吃了牛排锅地道好吃
·
第6️⃣天：上午欣赏额尔古纳草原初秋的湿地黄绿渐变河道蜿蜒，成群的牛马过水美的不像话，下午奔赴莫日格勒河俯瞰天下第一曲水壮阔又温柔，在落日余晖下我们疯狂拍照记录下开心时刻，返回海拉尔吃了心心念念的俄餐
第7️⃣天：自由行简单逛逛，吃地道的内蒙火锅，然后返程

items.text:
GTA 6 File Size Confirmed By Gameplay Leaker

Published Oct 13, 2026, 5:59 AM EDT

Paul Farrelly is a Contributing Writer for Screen Rant’s Gaming section and the founder of GeekGasm.org, a site dedicated to celebrating all things gaming, from triple A blockbusters to weird and wonderful indie hits. Based in Louth, Ireland, Paul has spent years writing about games, pop culture, and tech, turning his lifelong love of gaming into a career that lets him talk (probably too much) about what makes this industry so endlessly fascinating.
He’s previously written and collaborated with several entertainment outlets, including LADbible, gaining a wide perspective on how gaming fits into today’s pop culture conversation. His work blends genuine enthusiasm with thoughtful analysis, exploring how design, storytelling, and community have made gaming one of the most creative mediums around.
When he’s not glued to a controller or keyboard, Paul’s usually spinning vinyl, plotting his next horror marathon, or debating which Resident Evil entry really reigns supreme.

The launch of Grand Theft Auto VI is so close now, we can nearly taste the sprinkles off an ice cream on Vice Beach. But even though the 19 November 2026 is fast approaching, we're still crazing more content. Sure, the Netflix showcase called Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look, gave us a lot to comb through, but apart from that, Rockstar Games and, indeed, Take-Two Interactive have been only drip feeding us the smallest of tidbits.

Aside from official channels, there has been more content brought to light for fans wanting more. Cyberleek disappeared for a while when the Netflix Extended Look launched, but then came back even harder. They released their own Extended Leek to mimic what had come before. This similar in length leak, showed among other things, that Cyberleek had a working model of the game with developer mode enabled. Spawning in tanks and showing off characters going commando was perhaps a step too far for some fans.

One useful piece of information that has come from Cyberleek though is the game file size. It's useful because it lets us gamers know how much free space we need on our PS5 or XBox hard drives prior to launch. It also doesn't spoil the game in any way for purists who want to enjoy it fresh, which is a relief. In fact, knowing what the file size might be could help gamers avoid a failed download while they sleep. Imagine waking up hoping to play Grand Theft Auto VI on November 19 only to have a failed download message staring back at you.

As with all information from Cyberleek, this needs to be taken with a pinch of salt. Cyberleek has said they will leak the developer build they have if their meme coin reaches over $30 million in value and the file size they quote in their threat is more than 200GB. Bearing in mind though, they have a developer build which is most likely a lot chunkier and less optimized than the finished release. Players can expect the official release of the game to be smaller than 200GB. But, having this ballpark figure in mind, it will now be easier to keep at least 200GB hard drive space free before November 19, 2026.

YouTube

When you take into account Rockstar's last big game, Red Dead Redemption 2, the file size on consoles was up to 107GB and on PC it was a whopping 150GB. Grand Theft Auto VI having a file size close to 200GB doesn't sound too far from reality and anyone erring on the side of caution might want to consider keeping 200GB free on their hard drive prior to launch. After all, Grand Theft Auto VI is shaping up to be one of the largest, most detailed open world games of all time, so it makes sense to keep some space free for November.

With Grand Theft Auto VI already selling out over at Amazon, it's clearly going to be one of the biggest games of the decade, and we're not just talking about hard drive space! But with us still having over a month to wait for it, it may be a good time to dip back into Red Dead Online and perhaps try out the new Red Dead Redemption 2: Fear of the Dark content, just in time for spooky season. Between now and November 19, let's hope Cyberleek keeps quiet and doesn't follow through on their promise to leak Grand Theft Auto VI to the public. I personally, don't need any more spoilers and want to play the game with fresh eyes next month.

In over three years at Collider, senior author Jake has now penned over 3000 articles covering a wide range of TV and film for the resources, lists, utilities, news, and interview teams. Alongside interviewing stars such as Selin Hizli, Rose Ayling-Ellis, Harlan Coben, and Chelsea Peretti, Jake was lucky enough to visit the set of Aardman and Netflix's Wallace and Gromit: A Vengeance Most Fowl in 2024, getting the chance to chat with four-time Academy Award winner Nick Park and Merlin Crossingham. Jake has also worked for other publications, including Agents of Fandom. You can also hear Jake every week as the resident film and TV journalist on Track Radio.

Taking a glance at the Apple TV charts, one is immediately struck by the popularity of Ted Lasso. Following the show's fourth season finale this week, and with hopes high for a fifth season renewal, the beloved soccer series is edging closer to surpassing the 1,000-day mark on the Apple TV charts and will likely remain the most-watched show on the platform for a couple of weeks yet.

Characters such as Ted (Jason Sudeikis), Keeley (Juno Temple), Higgins (Jeremy Swift), and Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham) are some of the biggest ever to appear on Apple TV, with the titular coach arguably the face of the platform. The premiere of Season 4 even broke a record for Apple TV, earning a remarkable 296.6 million views during its first two days. But the dominance of Ted Lasso shouldn't distract from the other titles proving popular on the platform, with an unlikely 22-year-old sci-fi hit managing to surpass its own streaming milestone.

At the time of writing, I, Robot, the 2004 sci-fi thriller starring Will Smith, has surpassed the 50-day mark as part of the Apple TV top ten in the U.S. Also starring Bridget Moynahan, Bruce Greenwood, and even Alan Tudyk, I, Robot was based on Isaac Asimov's 1950 short story collection, which also inspired the acclaimed Apple TV series Foundation. I, Robot's arrival on Apple TV is part of the platform's expansion of its movie collection away from in-house features, with other sci-fi favorites such as E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial also proving popular.

Which Sci-Fi Hero Are You Most Like?
Paul Atreides · Captain Kirk · Princess Leia · Ellen Ripley · Max Rockatansky

Five iconic heroes. Five completely different ways of facing an impossible universe. One of them shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of refusing to back down. Eight questions will tell you which one.

🏜️Paul Atreides

🖖Capt. Kirk

✊Princess Leia

🔦Ellen Ripley

🔥Max Rockatansky

FIND YOUR HERO →

01

How do you lead when the stakes couldn't be higher?
The way you lead under pressure is the most honest thing about you.

AI absorb everything — every variable, every pattern — and move only when I know the path forward.
BI read the room, make the call, and own the consequences. Hesitation costs more than mistakes.
CI rally people. A cause needs a voice, and I refuse to let fear be louder than conviction.
DI assess the threat, establish what needs doing, and get it done without waiting for permission.
EI don't lead. I act. Others can follow or not — I'm already moving.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

What is your greatest strength in a crisis?
The quality that keeps you alive when everything else fails.

APrescience — the ability to see further ahead than anyone else and plan accordingly.
BImprovisation — I'm at my best when the plan falls apart and I have to invent a new one.
CConviction — I know what I'm fighting for, and that certainty doesn't waver under fire.
DComposure — I stay functional when everyone around me is falling apart. Panic is a luxury.
EEndurance — I outlast things. I take the hit and keep moving long after others have stopped.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What is the thing you'd sacrifice everything else for?
Your deepest motivation is your truest compass.

AThe survival and dignity of my people — even if I have to become something frightening to ensure it.
BThe safety of my crew — every single one of them. No one gets left behind.
CFreedom — for my people, for every world still crushed under the weight of an empire.
DThe truth — what actually happened, what's actually out there, whether anyone believes me or not.
EThe one person — or the one memory — that still makes any of this worth surviving for.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How do you relate to the people around you?
Who you are to others under pressure is who you really are.

AWith intensity and distance — I care deeply, but the weight I carry makes closeness complicated.
BWith warmth and irreverence — I take the mission seriously, not myself.
CWith directness and trust — I say what I mean, and I expect the people I work with to rise to it.
DWith professional care but clear limits — I'll protect you, but I won't pretend we're family.
EWith wariness that slowly becomes loyalty — I don't trust easily, but when I do, it holds.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

You're facing a threat that no one else believes is real. What do you do?

items.title: “Cupertino” is a Smart Big Tech Procedural
items.author: Jen Chaney
items.summary: Movie theaters are currently inundated with major motion pictures that examine and/or indict the behavior of wealthy Silicon Valley leaders, including Meta’s
items.text:
Movie theaters are currently inundated with major motion pictures that examine and/or indict the behavior of wealthy Silicon Valley leaders, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg (“The Social Reckoning”), Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes (“You Can See Everything”), Elon Musk (Alex Gibney’s “Musk”), and OpenAI’s Sam Altman (“Artificial”). Television is in on the trend, too. In November, Netflix will remind us of the implosion of cryptocurrency fund FTX and its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, in “The Altruists.”

On CBS and Paramount+ starting Thursday, there’s “Cupertino,” a broadcast-network procedural that doesn’t zero in on a real-life tech bro, but does raise a lot of sobering questions about the industry currently attempting to cram A.I. down the throats of the global populace.

Created by Michelle and Robert King—the showrunning power couple responsible for “The Good Wife,” “The Good Fight,” “Evil,” “Elsbeth,” and ensuring that CBS still offers quality programming in primetime—the series is a legal drama about an upstart law firm that focuses specifically on clients who want to sue powerful Silicon Valley companies.

“I’m sick of people controlling my fate, and my guess is there are a lot of people out there that feel the same way but don’t have anyone to represent them,” says Michael Price (Mike Colter of “Luke Cage” and “Evil”), an attorney who co-founded, then got edged out of, an extremely successful big tech company called S-Talk.

He’s explaining his reasons for wanting to start an agency that takes on the cases against Magnificent 7-level companies that other firms are too afraid to touch. But he could just as easily be describing this show’s appeal to an American audience frustrated by the unemployment rate, the disproportionate power and wealth of the billionaire class, and the non-stop insistence that everyone get on board with artificial intelligence.

Unlike the other projects mentioned above, “Cupertino” does not focus on the idiosyncrasies/neuroses of a single, perceived “genius.” It is more general in its depiction of big tech, which enables it to feel both timely and, perhaps, more relatable to the average person.

Pictured (L-R): Rachel Keller as Olivia Siffre and Mike Colter as Michael Price. Photo: Elizabeth Fisher/CBS ©2026 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. All Rights Reserved.

While there are some key storylines that run throughout the first 10 episodes—the rivalry between Michael and his showboating lawyer father (Joe Morton); another, separate rivalry between Michael and his ex, also an attorney (Renée Elise Goldsberry, who co-starred opposite Colter on “Evil”); and, most importantly, an ongoing narrative about a particularly dangerous form of AI—this is largely a case-of-the-week type of show.

With its quick, plot-driven pacing, “Cupertino” is episodic, mainstream network storytelling that shows, like so much of the Kings’ output, that it’s still possible to make smart, sophisticated, digestible television within that framework.

As Michael, Colter is dignified, pragmatic and, if I’m being honest, not wildly different in demeanor from David, the priest the actor played on “Evil.” But he’s a persuasive lead in both shows, so I’m not going to complain too much about any overlap. While Michael believes in justice and the rule of law, he’s not some anti-capitalist hero who wants to burn down all of Silicon Valley. He simply sees a gap in the marketplace that needs filling. “When you’re in the middle of the ocean, you don’t sell people more water,” he explains to Goldsberry’s Nichole. “You sell them life jackets.”

His partner at the new firm, Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller), a devout Christian and gifted lawyer who also gets fired from S-Talk after being sexually harassed by the head of the company, is the bleeding heart in this pairing. Keller and Colter have an organic, friendly chemistry that, to the show’s credit, is supportive without being romantic, at least not in these early episodes.

But the standout performances in “Cupertino” come from the two actors who provide the most comedic relief in a drama that doesn’t shy away from poking fun at the always-pitching culture of venture capitalism. Ella Stiller (daughter of Ben Stiller and Christine Taylor) gets a break-out role as Christy Palladino, a third employee who gets fired from S-Talk and becomes the receptionist at Price and Siffre, where she proves to be a fantastic investigator for her attorney bosses.

Christy is particularly adept at tracking down leads and calling in favors from her extensive family of blue-collar workers; after being escorted out of the S-Talk building, she phones her electrician uncle, who proceeds to turn the power on and off in that office and enrage everyone still “lucky” enough to be employed there. Christy knows nothing about technology, but she loves to stick it to the man. Her default expression is resting “you’ve got to be kidding me” face, and Stiller has got that expression down pat.

Pictured (L-R): Ella Stiller as Christy Palladino, Mike Colter as Michael Price, and Rachel Keller as Olivia Siffre. Photo: Elizabeth Fisher/CBS ©2026 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. All Rights Reserved

Then there’s Busy Phillips, who’s cast as Natalia Boutella, a key investor in the new firm who also happens to be divorced from a tech executive played by Fisher Stevens who is not Jeff Bezos, but also is totally Jeff Bezos. Created by Michelle and Robert King—the showrunning power couple responsible for “The Good Wife,” “The Good Fight,” “Evil,” “Elsbeth,” and ensuring that CBS still offers quality programming in primetime—the series is a legal drama about an upstart law firm that focuses specifically on clients who want to sue powerful Silicon Valley companies.

Tom Wilson is a Gaming Features Writer at Screen Rant. Over the past five years, Tom has worked as the Editor-in-Chief at The Game Crater, as a Staff Writer for GamingIntel, a List Writer at TheGamer, and, of course, as a Senior Writer at ScreenRant. Tom graduated with a Masters in Multimedia Journalism, and has since gone on to build up his portfolio of games journalism work.

Final Fantasy is currently on a historic run. Its critically acclaimed remake trilogy of the beloved Final Fantasy 7 is coming to its epic conclusion, with the final entry releasing in 2027; the series is making a historic return to its pixel art roots with Resonance; Final Fantasy 14's release on the Nintendo Switch 2 ushered in an influx of new fans, breathing new life into the already immensely popular MMO. Suffice it to say, if you're a fan of Final Fantasy, there should be absolutely no shortage of exciting new releases on the horizon.

Joining the many upcoming Final Fantasy projects is a smaller, yet nevertheless exciting, release titled Till My Dawn Tears Flow. The excessively named release will be perfect for those who love everything Final Fantasy and wish to celebrate it in every conceivable way. It's designed with fans in mind, delivering a hopefully emotional and epic experience that will be a memorable addition to absolutely any Final Fantasy fanatic's collection.

One of the best things to happen to Final Fantasy as of late was the aforementioned, tremendously successful Switch 2 FFXIV launch. It rejuvenated the game with an abundance of fresh new faces, all of whom were joining a largely friendly player base eager to help. Its prevalence on a Nintendo platform ushered in the final stage in FFXIV's dominance of the MMO market, further increasing its reach and scope and almost certainly ushering in a new age for the legendary and utterly transformed experience.

Conveniently timed around the launch of Final Fantasy 14 on the Nintendo Switch 2 is a plethora of exciting merchandise and collectibles for the game. However, these aren't merely the typical trinkets one would expect, although those are certainly on the cards. Rather, these upcoming Final Fantasy 14 projects offer fans a lot of meaningful substance or unique experiences hard to obtain elsewhere. Chief among these is the aforementioned Till My Dawn Tears Flow, a brand-new album featuring all-new arrangements of Final Fantasy 14's excellent soundtrack.

The Till My Dawn Tears Flow album is available for purchase via the official Square Enix website for $25.99.

The Till My Dawn Tears Flow album features eight tracks from Final Fantasy XIV rearranged for the piano, as well as a download code for a video of the Bee My Honey performance at the FFXIV Anaheim fan festival in 2026. The songs come on a CD imported from Japan and will be released in North America in November 2026, just shortly after the Japanese release on October 14, 2026. A more specific release date has yet to be confirmed. Here are all eight tracks, as well as the song Promises to Keep from the album:

01. Lost in the Deep

02. Morrow’s Might & Magic

03. Roses of May (Dawntrail)

04. Crash in the Dark

05. Smile

06. Windswept Echoes

07. Promises to Keep

08. Bee My Honey

While this album may not be the major project some are likely hoping for, it does provide fans with yet another unique way of interacting with their favorite game. Final Fantasy's merchandise can be hit or miss, with some titles receiving little more than puzzle sets, while others get bespoke music boxes and unique statues. It's hard to argue that this collection of beautiful tracks from Final Fantasy 14 is a loss. At the very least, hopefully, when it launches in November, truly dedicated Final Fantasy fans will enjoy it.

'Rick and Morty' Creator's Horror Cult Classic Officially Haunts a New Streamming Home

Image via Sony Pictures Releasing

Animated movies have been giving children reasons to sleep with the lights on for generations. The Nightmare Before Christmas made a Christmas delivery genuinely threatening, while Coraline turned the promise of a better home into a particularly convincing nightmare. Their characters might look inviting on a poster, but watching the movies is another matter. A family-friendly rating doesn’t guarantee that everyone will leave feeling reassured.

That’s part of what makes those movies so satisfying to revisit in October. They take childhood fears seriously enough to build a story around them, even when the adults onscreen would prefer to dismiss the problem. Being small and having no one believe you is frightening before anything supernatural happens. Give those children a monster to deal with, and suddenly the adventure has considerably higher stakes than getting grounded.

Monster House is finding a Halloween audience on Peacock twenty years after its 2006 release. According to a U.S. movie chart, the animated horror comedy sits at No. 3, directly behind Coraline. It ranks above Trolls Band Together and How the Grinch Stole Christmas, with Casper also appearing in the top ten. That gives Peacock two unsettling animated adventures in its top three, making this a particularly good month for movies that taught their youngest viewers to be suspicious of perfectly ordinary homes.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
Which Netflix Character Would Be Your Best Friend?
Dustin · Emily · Wednesday · Gi-hun

Some friends drag you out of the house. Some sit with you on the worst night of your life. Netflix has written both, plus the one who tells you the truth you have been avoiding all week. Answer eight quick questions about how you actually do friendship, and find out which of them was always going to end up in your corner.

🧢Dustin(Stranger Things)

🗼Emily(Emily in Paris)

🕷️Wednesday(Wednesday)

🟢Gi-hun(Squid Game)

FIND YOUR BEST FRIEND →

01

How do you usually end up making a new friend?
The origin story says a lot about the friendship that follows it.

AWe got loud about the same obsession and never stopped.
BThey invited me somewhere before we had properly met.
CWe bonded over disliking exactly the same thing.
DThey noticed I was struggling and stayed with me.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

What is a perfect Saturday with your best friend?
Friendship is mostly built out of very ordinary hours.

AA ridiculous plan neither of us should attempt.
BSomewhere new, photographed heavily, ending very late.
CSomewhere quiet, few people, zero small talk.
DSomething simple, and a conversation that actually matters.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

You call them at two in the morning. What happens?
This is the real test of a friendship, and everybody knows it.

AThey are already putting their shoes on.
BThey answer instantly and turn it into a plan.
CThey answer and say something unflattering and true.
DThey listen for an hour and never check the time.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

What do you want from them when you are clearly wrong?
The best friendships are the ones that survive being corrected.

ASupport first. We can review the mistake later.
BA relentlessly positive reframe of the entire disaster.
CThe blunt version. Do not soften it for me.
DPatience, and no judgment about how I got here.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

What do your friends actually value about you?
The friend you attract says something about the friend you are.

AI am all in, always, about everything.
BI can turn almost any situation into a good time.
CI say the thing nobody else in the room will.
DI look after whoever is having the worst day.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

You have a falling out. How does it go?
How a friendship repairs itself matters more than how it breaks.

ALoudly, briefly, then back to normal by Tuesday.
BThey apologise first, enthusiastically, with a gift.
CCold silence, then one dry joke that fixes everything.
DWe talk until we both understand what actually happened.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

What do you actually need a best friend for?
Everybody is missing something. The right friend fills that gap.

ATo make my life bigger than it would be alone.
BTo push me out of the house and into my own life.
CTo catch me when I start lying to myself.
DTo be the person who never gave up on me.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

Ten years from now, what keeps the two of you close?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides who you get.

AWe would still drop everything for each other, instantly.
BWe still make plans, and we still actually go.
CWe still cut through each other's nonsense in one sentence.
DThey stood by me once when it cost them something.

REVEAL MY BEST FRIEND →

The Group Chat Has Spoken
Your Best Friend Is…

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up
for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your
life would be like.

Stranger Things · Netflix · Since 2016

Dustin Henderson

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he.
What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the
plan.

Dustin is the friend the entire show runs on: loyal past the point of sense,
enthusiastic about everything, and incapable of leaving anybody behind.

You have the same instinct. Your friendships are loud, specific and slightly ridiculous,
and they last for decades because of it.

He is also the one person who would take your strangest interest completely seriously,
which is far rarer than it sounds.

You would have a group chat. It would never once be quiet.

Emily in Paris · Netflix · Since 2020

Emily Cooper

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she.
Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with
yourselves.

Emily treats an ordinary Tuesday as something that could be turned into an occasion,
which is either the best or the worst quality in a friend depending on your energy
levels.

You share her refusal to sit still. Neither of you has ever accepted a night in when
something was happening somewhere else.

She is far more loyal than people give her credit for. She defends her friends loudly,
publicly, and occasionally before checking the facts.

She would post the photo without asking. You would forgive her, because it is a very
good photo.

Wednesday · Netflix · Since 2022

Wednesday Addams

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to
tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this
list.

Wednesday never says a kind thing she does not mean, which makes the rare ones count for
an enormous amount.

You would rather be told the truth than be made comfortable. She is constitutionally
incapable of offering you anything else.

Underneath all of it she is ferociously protective. She simply refuses to make a
performance out of caring.

Do not expect a birthday message. Do expect her to ruin anyone who wrongs you.

Squid Game · Netflix · 2021–2025

Seong Gi-hun

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is
the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Gi-hun is not the strongest player in Squid Game, or the cleverest. He is the one who
keeps choosing to protect somebody else, over and over, at genuine cost to himself.

You have the same instinct. You notice who is struggling and you stay with them, long
after anybody would blame you for leaving.

He is a flawed friend, and that is part of why it lands. He lets people down, then comes
back and tries again, which is more than most manage.

He would give you his last chance and never once mention that he had done it.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

‘Monster House’ Makes the Creepy Neighbor the Least of the Kids’ Problems

Image via Columbia Pictures

Directed by Gil Kenan, the movie follows D.J., a boy keeping an eye on the intimidating house across the street. Its owner, Horace Nebbercracker, already gives the neighborhood children plenty of reasons to keep their distance. When D.J. discovers that the building itself is alive, he teams up with Chowder and Jenny to investigate. Mitchel Musso, Sam Lerner, and Spencer Locke voice the children, while Steve Buscemi plays Nebbercracker.

The premise takes a familiar childhood warning and gives it teeth. Staying off someone’s lawn becomes a matter of survival, and the house makes crossing the street look like a very poor decision. There’s comedy in the children’s arguments and questionable plans, but it never makes the threat feel harmless. The movie commits to making its monster scary, which is exactly what gives the adventure something worth overcoming.

It also understands how much danger changes when the characters have limited options. D.J. and his friends can’t simply call someone who will immediately accept that a house is trying to eat people. They have to investigate a threat they barely understand while knowing that getting closer could make them its next victims. That puts viewers in the uncomfortable position of wanting answers and wanting the children to stay as far away as possible.

Monster House is available to stream on Peacock.

Their characters might look inviting on a poster, but watching the movies is another matter. A family-friendly rating doesn’t guarantee that everyone will leave feeling reassured.

That’s part of what makes those movies so satisfying to revisit in October. They take childhood fears seriously enough to build a story around them, even when the adults onscreen would prefer to dismiss the problem. Being small and having no one believe you is frightening before anything supernatural happens. Give those children a monster to deal with, and suddenly the adventure has considerably higher stakes than getting grounded.

Monster House is finding a Halloween audience on Peacock twenty years after its 2006 release. According to a U.S. movie chart, the animated horror comedy sits at No. 3, directly behind Coraline. It ranks above Trolls Band Together and How the Grinch Stole Christmas, with Casper also appearing in the top ten. That gives Peacock two unsettling animated adventures in its top three, making this a particularly good month for movies that taught their youngest viewers to be suspicious of perfectly ordinary homes.

Known as 'Cyberpunk 2077's' biggest fan, Angharad is a Welsh games writer who thrives in anything related to digital storytelling. If a video game explores the intricacies and horrors of womanhood, she is there.
Thanks to previous work at GAMINGbible, GameByte, The Loadout, Game Luster, Angharad has built a strong understanding of both the digital world and what fans want from it and is eager to share her thoughts and expertise with readers.

Cementing himself as one of the most memorable fictional characters in history, Jon Snow is set to make a triumphant return this month. It has been seven years since we last saw him become one of the few characters to survive Game of Thrones as he returned to the Wall following the events of the much-talked-about finale.

As the Bastard of Winterfell, Jon Snow did not do too bad for himself. Not only did he climb the ranks of the Nightswatch, return from the dead, and find love, but he also discovered that, alongside Daenerys, he was the last remaining Targaryen. We can only hope that his luck is as strong in Winds of Winter, if and when the next book in the A Song of Ice and Fire saga is released.

For now, however, Game of Thrones' influence certainly did not die with the show as, since it ended back in 2019, HBO has released two spin-off shows: House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, and that is not to mention Aegon's Conquest, which is currently in production.

On top of that, the video game sphere has also been jumping on the bandwagon with hit mobile games such as Game of Thrones: Legends leading the charge whilst fans wait for the launch of Game of Thrones: War for Westeros, a real-time strategy title which is expected to launch some time in 2027.

It is Game of Thrones: Legends that is the subject of today's news, as it appears as though Jon Snow will be making his triumphant return in an event which is currently running on the hit mobile RPG.

The Game of Thrones-inspired mobile game was released back in 2024 by Zynga and has since welcomed regular content updates which correspond with the ever-growing television universe. As such, players can expect to see characters and events from both House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, as well as Game of Thrones, and as the ASOIAF universe continues to grow, no doubt this game will also expand.

At the time of writing, the September-October 2026 events for Game of Thrones: Legends are still in full swing, and on top of brand-new quests, locations, and characters, it seems as though the Hand of the King event, which runs from 23 September to 21 October, at 2 a.m. ET, will see the return of not just Jon Snow, but also Ned Stark, Sansa Stark, Arya Stark, Rob Stark, and Catelyn Stark. Known as Legendary Champions, they will be able to be summoned with exalted tokens, and will no doubt make an invaluable part of your team.

With the event calendar for the month coming to an end for Game of Thrones: Legends, we can no doubt expect the next roadmap to be announced very soon, and so, if you were thinking of sinking some hours into another mobile game, you will not find more content than in this Game of Thrones-inspired hit.

items.text:
We can admit it: Star Wars fans really love Jedi, and they are especially fun to play as in video games. Jedi: Fallen Order and Jedi: Survivor are recent Star Wars games featuring Jedi Cal Kestis, and they are beloved for their action-packed lightsaber-wielding, Force-powered gameplay. Now in 2026, we have not one, but two Star Wars games that have cleared Respawn Entertainment's Jedi series on Metacritic. Star Wars Zero Company, co-developed by Bit Reactor and Respawn, launched in August to a score of 86. Star Wars: Galactic Racer followed it up this month with an 88, making it the highest-rated Star Wars release since Knights of the Old Republic in 2003. And here's the kicker: neither title stars a Force-sensitive protagonist.

These two games actually share a lot in common. Both are debut releases from brand-new studios built by genre specialists: Bit Reactor, founded by modern XCOM veterans, and Fuse Games, founded by Criterion veterans who worked on the Burnout series. Both teams stuck to the style of game they knew best and brought that expertise into the Star Wars universe. And it worked very well for both games. Lucasfilm Games and Disney moved away from EA exclusivity, and this decision seems to be paying off. These games may never match the sales numbers of EA's biggest Star Wars blockbusters, but they show the franchise can work in many more genres beyond the action-adventure and FPS focus of the last decade.

What really makes 2026's Star Wars releases interesting is how they both rebuild a fractured legacy. Instead of following the tried-and-true formulas already established by past Star Wars titles, Zero Company and Galactic Racer essentially act as revivals of dormant franchises. Bit Reactor and Fuse Games utilized their opportunity to make a Star Wars game to spiritually revive XCOM and Burnout at the same time.

Firaxis released XCOM 2 in 2016, and that was the last mainline entry followed only by the smaller Chimera Squad. Burnout has been dormant for much longer, with Burnout Paradise landing in 2008 right before the studio consolidated into the Need for Speed machine. While the publishers who owned these golden franchises sat on them like a mother goose, the talent behind them left and formed their own studios. Greg Foertsch, art director of the modern XCOM games, left Firaxis to start Bit Reactor and filled it with former colleagues, while Matt Webster, former GM of Criterion Games, started Fuse Games with other Criterion developers who worked on Burnout and Need for Speed.

They weren't recruited to put their spin on Star Wars Outlaws or The Force Unleashed. Bit Reactor and Fuse Games were tasked to do what they do best and bring that to a galaxy far, far away. Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order and Survivor were great cinematic action-adventure games that took that formula to heights we hadn't seen before. Those games had to have mass appeal and cater to a wider, broader audience in order to succeed. Zero Company and Galactic Racer only had to strike a chord with the niche fanbases who hadn't had a real fix in years.

That's the secret behind these high-scoring titles. Another major boon is that while Burnout and XCOM may have been too niche for today's audience, the Star Wars license brings new fans to the genre that probably would never have touched it otherwise. And it isn't like they just slapped a Star Wars skin on and called it a day; these games meld with the universe perfectly. Zero Company's mercenary group and permadeath mechanics showcase a new side of the Clone Wars, making it feel costly. The lawless Outer Rim is also a natural fit for underground racing in Galactic Racer. Two dead franchises found new life, and Star Wars got two of its best games in 20 years out of the deal.

Related

Among Star Wars Royalty

Image via Nintendo

An 88 and an 86 are remarkable numbers for this franchise, and that places them in reach of some legendary games. There are only four Star Wars games that have the high ground, and that proves how good fans have it in 2026. They were able to pull off a feat that EA couldn't with a decade of exclusivity.

At the top sits Knights of the Old Republic with an impressive 94, and 23 years later it is still the gold standard. A sprawling BioWare RPG set in the Old Republic with one of the best twists in gaming history, it's no wonder it hasn't been dethroned. 1997's Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II holds a 91; it's an amazing first-person shooter that introduced first-person lightsaber combat and Force abilities. Rogue Squadron II: Rogue Leader earned a 90 as a GameCube launch title and remains the definitive Star Wars flight experience. Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast rounds it out at 89 with the best Jedi combat gaming has ever witnessed.

That is the collective Galactic Racer now sits directly beneath, one point behind Jedi Outcast and ahead of everything else the license has produced in two decades. Zero Company isn't far behind, tying Knights of the Old Republic II at 86. For both games to be debut launches from fresh studios, being in that conversation is extraordinary.

Star Wars Zero Company and Star Wars: Galactic Racer prove something the franchise seemed to forget: this galaxy is vast enough to tell unique stories without relying on the greatest hits. A tactics game about an expendable mercenary outfit and an arcade racer around underground syndicates have nothing to do with Jedi or the Skywalkers, and they're now the franchise's highest-rated games in over 20 years. That doesn't mean Jedi games are bad, far from it, in fact. Jedi: Survivor is an excellent game, and the next one will likely be too. The lesson is that it's time to take Star Wars gaming in new directions, and Lucasfilm Games seems to be figuring that out as well. The franchise can work in just about any genre, so I hope to see this trend continue until Star Wars reaches every genre imaginable.

What really makes 2026's Star Wars releases interesting is how they both rebuild a fractured legacy. Instead of following the tried-and-true formulas already established by past Star Wars titles, Zero Company and Galactic Racer essentially act as revivals of dormant franchises. Bit Reactor and Fuse Games utilized their opportunity to make a Star Wars game to spiritually revive XCOM and Burnout at the same time.

Firaxis released XCOM 2 in 2016, and that was the last mainline entry followed only by the smaller Chimera Squad. Burnout has been dormant for much longer, with Burnout Paradise landing in 2008 right before the studio consolidated into the Need for Speed machine. While the publishers who owned these golden franchises sat on them like a mother goose, the talent behind them left and formed their own studios. Greg Foertsch, art director of the modern XCOM games, left Firaxis to start Bit Reactor and filled it with former colleagues, while Matt Webster, former GM of Criterion Games, started Fuse Games with other Criterion developers who worked on Burnout and Need for Speed.

They weren't recruited to put their spin on Star Wars Outlaws or The Force Unleashed. Bit Reactor and Fuse Games were tasked to do what they do best and bring that to a galaxy far, far away. Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order and Survivor were great cinematic action-adventure games that took that formula to heights we hadn't seen before. Those games had to have mass appeal and cater to a wider, broader audience in order to succeed. Zero Company and Galactic Racer only had to strike a chord with the niche fanbases who hadn't had a real fix in years.

That's the secret behind these high-scoring titles. Another major boon is that while Burnout and XCOM may have been too niche for today's audience, the Star Wars license brings new fans to the genre that probably would never have touched it otherwise. And it isn't like they just slapped a Star Wars skin on and called it a day; these games meld with the universe perfectly. Zero Company's mercenary group and permadeath mechanics showcase a new side of the Clone Wars, making it feel costly. The lawless Outer Rim is also a natural fit for underground racing in Galactic Racer. Two dead franchises found new life, and Star Wars got two of its best games in 20 years out of the deal.

An 88 and an 86 are remarkable numbers for this franchise, and that places them in reach of some legendary games. There are only four Star Wars games that have the high ground, and that proves how good fans have it in 2026. They were able to pull off a feat that EA couldn't with a decade of exclusivity.

At the top sits Knights of the Old Republic with an impressive 94, and 23 years later it is still the gold standard. A sprawling BioWare RPG set in the Old Republic with one of the best twists in gaming history, it's no wonder it hasn't been dethroned. 1997's Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II holds a 91; it's an amazing first-person shooter that introduced first-person lightsaber combat and Force abilities. Rogue Squadron II: Rogue Leader earned a 90 as a GameCube launch title and remains the definitive Star Wars flight experience. Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast rounds it out at 89 with the best Jedi combat gaming has ever witnessed.

That is the collective Galactic Racer now sits directly beneath, one point behind Jedi Outcast and ahead of everything else the license has produced in two decades. Zero Company isn't far behind, tying Knights of the Old Republic II at 86. For both games to be debut launches from fresh studios, being in that conversation is extraordinary.

Star Wars Zero Company and Star Wars: Galactic Racer prove something the franchise seemed to forget: this galaxy is vast enough to tell unique stories without relying on the greatest hits. A tactics game about an expendable mercenary outfit and an arcade racer around underground syndicates have nothing to do with Jedi or the Skywalkers, and they're now the franchise's highest-rated games in over 20 years. That doesn't mean Jedi games are bad, far from it, in fact. Jedi: Survivor is an excellent game, and the next one will likely be too. The lesson is that it's time to take Star Wars gaming in new directions, and Lucasfilm Games seems to be figuring that out as well. The franchise can work in just about any genre, so I hope to see this trend continue until Star Wars reaches every genre imaginable.

items.text:
Nintendo Switch 2 Drops Free Download For 10/10 Masterpiece JRPG

Custom image by Katarina Cimbaljevic

Published Oct 13, 2026, 4:07 AM EDT

Bruno Yonezawa is a Gaming Senior Writer for Screen Rant. He's been practicing professional journalism for over 10 years, and is also a communications specialist. He's played games all his life and turned that passionate hobby into a passionate career, in an industry where he's worked as a writer, editor, analyst, and more.

A free download for a 10/10 masterpiece JRPG has just been officially dropped on Nintendo Switch 2, and if you’re a fan of the genre, you’ll want to make sure you don’t miss this freebie. While tons of exclusive games are being released for Nintendo’s current-gen hardware, we’re also seeing several previously available titles enhanced and re-released for the platform. For example, the first two Octopath Traveler games joined Nintendo Switch 2 this month, offering improved graphics, enhanced frame rates, and much more. These ports are continuously being added to the Switch 2 ecosystem.

Now we’re getting a new one. Ahead of the port’s official release on Nintendo Switch 2 in November, a free download for this 10/10 JRPG has been made available. As was reported by RPG Site, the demo for the upcoming game is now available, and you can download and play it entirely for free. The Prologue Demo represents the very beginning of the full version of the game, and its save data can be transferred into the game, should you choose to purchase and play it.

The demo in question is for the Metaphor: ReFantazio port for Nintendo Switch 2. On its product page in the Nintendo eShop, where you can pre-order the game, you can instead opt to download the demo. This is entirely free, no strings attached. The only issue is that you may need to open up some storage space, as the demo’s download size is reportedly 29.8 GB. This will be the first time the game will be playable on the Nintendo ecosystem, as it was not released for the original Nintendo Switch.

The game’s port for Nintendo Switch 2 was announced during this June’s Nintendo Direct event, the same presentation that confirmed the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, showcased a new Kingdom Hearts 4 trailer, and more. Metaphor: ReFantazio will be officially released for Nintendo Switch 2 on November 12 this year, so playing the demo right now could be a great way of getting yourself ready for the huge JRPG adventure to come.

Feature Image Credit: Katarina Cimbaljevic

Metaphor: ReFantazio is a turn-based JRPG from the creators of Persona 3, Persona 4, and Persona 5. In fact, there are several similarities between this new IP and Persona – so much so that Metaphor: ReFantazio is often described as a high fantasy Persona. Released in 2024 for PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC, Metaphor: ReFantazio redefined JRPGs, becoming one of the best games that year.

If you haven’t played this game yet, checking it out via its new free demo may be the way to go. Metaphor: ReFantazio is certainly worth the time, and if you’re already a fan of JRPGs, playing it on Nintendo Switch 2 may be the ultimate experience.

items.text:
Invincible Returns Winter 2026 With New VS Release

Published Oct 13, 2026, 2:00 AM EDT

Jared is a writer, editor, and Communications Studies graduate who loves popular nerd culture (almost anything to do with Marvel, DC, Star Wars, or The Lord of the Rings) and the interactive storytelling medium. Jared's first console was the PS1, wherein he fell for Spider-Man, Spyro the Dragon, and Crash Bandicoot.

Like The Boys, Invincible is popularly known for its TV series adaptation and the fact that it tells a story about superheroes, though it’s hardly a ‘superhero story’ in the traditional sense, and it relishes in its ability to distinguish itself with graphic content. It’s a spoof on classic superhero stories, sure, but the charm of Invincible’s worldbuilding and characters is where it truly shines amid the mature language and dark humor that’ll pique your interest.

Invincible Season 5 is reportedly slated to premiere in 2027. Until then, though, fans are about to enjoy Season 2 of Invincible VS, a 3v3 tag fighting game adaptation of the Invincible universe, and it even has its own original campaign story. Plus, this holiday season, Invincible VS is officially adding a long-awaited character who is more than vaguely familiar to Marvel fans.

As per Twitter/X, Invincible VS announced that Agent Spider, Invincible’s legally distinct Spider-Man, will be added to the fighting game’s roster this winter. This means he won’t be available as a playable roster character until Season 3, but it’s great to hear that he’s a confirmed roster character in Invincible’s post-launch DLC, and winter 2026 is only a couple of months from now, anyway.

Agent Spider is largely an interesting character due to the obvious crossover of Marvel’s Spider-Man, who has already met Mark Grayson’s Invincible in a Marvel Team-Up crossover comic from Image. Moreover, Agent Spider is voiced by Josh Keaton, who voices the character in the animated series and famously plays Spider-Man in numerous projects, including the beloved Spectacular Spider-Man cartoon and the underrated video game Spider-Man: Edge of Time.

According to Invincible VS’ DLC roadmap, Agent Spider will be released in December, alongside new cosmetics, a new arena, quality-of-life updates, and a new Ranked season. Of course, Angstrom Levy arrives in Invincible VS today, though the Agent Spider announcement might’ve robbed him of his thunder a little bit. For the last little while, Invincible VS’ marketing on social media has been sharing gameplay and tips for how to play Angstrom Levy when he is released, and fans can likely expect the same sort of promotional material for Agent Spider when the Invincible character launches in December.

There are still a ton of iconic Invincible characters that fans can’t wait to see get adapted into Invincible VS. Funny enough, players will soon have a competent equivalent to Spider-Man to lab, and only time will tell if he’ll be as good as Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls’ Spider-Man. Agent Spider was probably one of the fighting game’s most highly anticipated Invincible characters, and it’ll be neat to see what competitive, high-level players think of him, much less who he might best be paired with in a 3v3 team composition.

items.title: A heartbreaking John Turturro steals The Only Living Pickpocket In New York
items.author: Monica Castillo
items.summary: For too long, John Turturro’s dependable talent has been taken for granted, which makes it all the better that he gets to shine in a great little drama like
items.text:
For too long, John Turturro’s dependable talent has been taken for granted, which makes it all the better that he gets to shine in a great little drama like Noah Segan’s The Only Living Pickpocket In New York. Showing off how great he’s always been, the veteran actor plays Harry, a classy kind of con man with nimble fingers and chummy rapport with fellow old-timers, like the NYPD officer who knows him better than most, Detective Warren (Giancarlo Esposito), and his best bud, a pawnbroker named Ben (Steve Buscemi). When he’s not pilfering wallets and watches off straphangers on the subway, Harry is looking after his ailing wife, Rosie (Karina Arroyave). But in a world of newfangled tech and digital dollars, Harry finds himself increasingly out of step with the game, especially when he steals the wrong bitcoin wallet off a dangerous brat named Dylan (Will Price).


Written and directed by Segan (Blood Relatives), The Only Living Pickpocket In New York is both a love letter to the city and a tribute to its toughness. It has a 1970s gloom—an awareness of how much harder it’s gotten to survive in one of the most expensive cities in the country, but also an awareness that in some ways, it’s always been hard to make it here. The movie mostly takes place over the course of one day, spanning from the Bronx to Manhattan’s Chinatown and later Queens and back again, speaking both to the city’s enormity and Harry’s isolation as he finds himself deeper and deeper in trouble. Yet, despite those problems, Harry finds moments of solidarity and community among strangers and friends, a kind of makeshift camaraderie in the face of a very bad day.


In addition to touching on the city’s affordability crisis, Segan’s script is also concerned with how new technology has left some generations behind. Harry isn’t just slowing down with age, it’s that the whole career of pickpocketing has changed, which can feel deeply relatable to those of use who have seen our fields completely reimagined in the past few decades, especially since the encroachment of generative AI. Harry feels obsolete in the digital age, and tries to ignore it until his ignorance lands him afoul of a crime family and their enterprising nepo baby.


Throughout these struggles, Turturro gives his character life and nuance. Harry is a heartbreaker, sad-eyed but mischievous. He’s got a wry sense of humor, but so much regret when it comes to his estranged daughter Kelly (Tatiana Maslany), whom he shares one long, overdue, tearful conversation with before cashing in his chips. He’s like a Robert Mitchum figure in a neo-noir picture, carrying a stoic but doomed sense of fatalism once he realizes he’s crossed the wrong folks. He’s a marked man, but one that will still go out according to his own gentleman criminal code. It’s not like Turturro hasn’t turned in great, nuanced performances before. It’s that The Only Living Pickpocket In New York leaves him in the spotlight for so much of the movie that Turturro can do what he does best: Act to every seat in the house with strong yet measured emotions, injecting a sense of realism into a New York City fable.


This kind of scrappy, small-scale drama used to regularly play in theaters back in the economic slump of the ‘70s, and maybe they’re making a comeback because audiences are hungrier for relatable heroes—everyday people with everyday problems, not superpowers. The Only Living Pickpocket In New York has the sadness of movies like The Friends Of Eddie Coyle and Fat City, with Turturro as the pitch-perfect underdog back in the mix for one last job. Segan’s view of the city feels expansive—not just limited to midtown and downtown, but a place where an actor like Turturro can live many lives onscreen—which means that his lead can bring new parts of the city to life through his reflections of it.

Writer: Noah Segan

Starring: John Turturro, Steve Buscemi, Giancarlo Esposito, Will Price, Tatiana Maslany, Jamie Lee Curtis, Victoria Moroles, Karina Arroyave

items.title: Gateway to Culture: How Meet Your Art Festival 2026 Connects Art, Music and Daily Life
items.author: Alina Joan Ito
items.summary: Celebrating its fifth anniversary in the waterfront district of Tennoz Canal, Meet Your Art Festival (MYAF) has grown into one of Japan’s premier art
items.text:
Celebrating its fifth anniversary in the waterfront district of Tennoz Canal, Meet Your Art Festival (MYAF) has grown into one of Japan’s premier art gatherings, attracting a whopping 50,000 visitors during its 2025 edition. The expanded Meet Your Art Festival 2026, running from October 9 to 12, will bring together over 150 artists, transforming warehouse galleries, floating canal stages and open-air markets into a sensory celebration of art, music, craft and food.

At its core, MYAF was built around a singular mission: to strip away the intimidating exclusivity of fine art and create as many entry points into contemporary culture as possible. Coming from the music industry, co-representative Yuri Kogo noticed a striking imbalance. “Musicians have a lot of opportunities to perform and plenty of streaming platforms and media,” she says. “I wanted to bring that accessibility for visual artists to showcase their work and meet new audiences.”

MYAF was launched to build that missing bridge, using food, fashion and live performances as inviting gateways for a broader audience to discover contemporary art. Crucially, the festival also aims to reshape societal values — elevating contemporary art from an elite hobby into a viable, respected career path for the next generation of creators.

YURI KOGO. PHOTOGRAPH BY COREY NICKOLS

Physicality and the ‘Reflux’ of Modern Times

This year’s central art exhibition, “Reflux: Rising Signs,” is directed by multidisciplinary artist Mirai Moriyama. Exploring the concept of counter-currents in our fast-paced digital age, the exhibition incorporates physical performances — from contemporary dance to martial arts to butoh-style movement — under Moriyama’s innovative vision. “In a world full of economic troubles and societal noise,” Kogo notes, “I think art has the power to make people stand still, take things in and look at things from a different perspective.”

Rather than just observing a painting propped on a wall, visitors are invited to physically interact with six body-focused performances, including those by artists Kana Kitty, Saori Hala and Contact Gonzo. “For one performance, the artists are going to use their bodies to create a wave-like movement with the audience, incorporating sound design, mirrors and video. I think it will be a space where attendees can really focus on their relationship to their bodies.”

By weaving together physical movement, acoustic resonance and spatial video, the entire exhibition becomes an immersive, multisensory environment where visitors physically participate and get to explore their immediate reaction to the art around them.

Beyond the live performances of “Reflux: Rising Signs,” the festival’s talk sessions provide yet another avenue for deep communion with art. Held at What Cafe, conversations with exhibiting artists, curators and guest commentators explore art in contemporary society, touching on music, fashion, urban life and culture while discussing topics as diverse as how to reinterpret ukiyo-e and the relationship between art and the brain. Note that sessions are conducted in Japanese.

Genre Crossover: Music and Subculture Meet Contemporary Art

MYAF’s identity relies on breaking down the traditional “white cube” gallery experience in favor of an immersive environment where different subcultures collide. Across the canal, the T-Lotus M floating stage anchors the site with live installations and DJ sets, providing a sonic experience unlike anything you’d expect at an art festival.

A centerpiece of this cross-disciplinary approach is a collaboration between legendary 90s music producer Tetsuya Komuro and contemporary artist Rintaro Fuse. “Komuro has made so much instantly recognizable music from the 1990s to the 2000s — he himself is a living archive,” says Kogo. She highlights how Fuse, who was still a baby during Komuro’s rise, is taking on the unique challenge of composing a live installation based on Komuro’s musical legacy, making for an extraordinary collaboration between prominent artists of two generations.

That same boundary-pushing energy continues inside the gallery halls. Ranging from rare vintage pop portraiture to experimental street fashion, the Co-Crossover art fair blends fine art with edgy subcultures under one roof. For Kogo, mixing these mediums creates crucial entry points for the public. “Music and street culture have a knack for grabbing large audiences, while contemporary art digs deeper into the human experience,” says Kogo, emphasizing how both worlds can learn from each other. By blending fashion, sound and subculture into one art gathering, MYAF strives to welcome crowds who might otherwise feel intimidated by traditional galleries.

Next door to Co-Crossover, the Meet Your Artists art fair exhibits approximately 500 works from over 40 artists at various stages in their careers, from up-and-comers to established creatives known at home and abroad. As the name suggests, Meet Your Artists is a chance for festivalgoers to interact with creators, getting to know the minds behind the masterpieces. With artworks available for purchase, visitors also have the chance to acquire pieces for their personal collections.

Bringing Contemporary Craft Home

Beyond the galleries, the festival grounds come alive with the Super Art & Craft Market, co-produced with Beams Creative. Presenting 80 shops spanning art merchandise, crafts and gastronomy, the market reinterprets traditional Japanese craftsmanship with a modern aesthetic. “At the craft market, you can understand the Japanese craftsmanship scene in a single location,” says Kogo.

From folk art books and artisanal ceramics to gelato from a Kyoto tea stand and a special ramen collaboration from Kumamoto, food and lifestyle lovers are offered yet another welcoming doorway into the art world. Kogo explains, “Our goal has always been to have as many people as possible experience art, which is why we gathered so many points of interest.”

While MYAF is already Japan’s largest art festival, Kogo envisions it becoming a global cultural benchmark. “I want to make it a world-famous festival — a prototype where you can experience the entire cultural scene of Japan in one place,” says Kogo. To turn this vision into reality, MYAF fosters direct connection: By encouraging visitors to chat directly with creators at the Meet Your Artists fair, the festival works to normalize art collecting and change mindsets around creative careers.

“I want to get rid of the idea that art isn’t a sustainable job,” says Kogo. “I hope to spread the message that art is a deeply respected profession, giving artists a global platform where their work and values are celebrated.”

More Info

Location: Tennoz Canal area, Tokyo (Warehouse Terrada, T-Lotus M, What Cafe, Boardwalk)

Tickets and Details: Meet Your Art Festival Official Site

items.title: 35 English Loanwords That Come From the Japanese Language
items.author: Coto Academy Staff Writer
items.summary: While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly
items.text:
While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly used that it might be easy to forget that they’re loanwords from Japan.

Let’s discover some common Japanese loanwords in English, covering some of the old and some of the new, but this blog is by no means exhaustive. By the end of this article, who knows? New words are probably being borrowed at this very moment.

Why Do Japanese and English Borrow so Many Words From Each Other?

Since Japanese and English come from very different places with distinct cultures, cuisines, and geographic characteristics or phenomena, the more exposed we are to each other’s cultures, the more new concepts and words we encounter. It makes sense that English would just adopt the words for Japanese food items like “sushi” or “ramen.”

However, the word tsunami is also of Japanese origin. It just so happens that English had no word for huge tidal waves, so it borrowed tsunami from Japanese. Often when a word sufficiently describes something we don’t have a word for, we just adopt it into our language. As you are probably well aware, Japanese quite often does the same.

You’ve probably experienced what could be called the katakana glitch. You see a katakana word, and you just can’t figure out what it is until you mouth it, then you finally figure out that biiru (ビール) is actually “beer”. You probably can think of many more English loanwords in Japanese, such as soccer, or sakkaa (サッカー), and even modern slang like rizz, or rizu (リズ). New words are crossing over, perhaps because the internet and pop culture spread new trends faster than ever before.

Note that this doesn’t always happen; when baseball was introduced to Japan, they made their own word for the sport, yakyuu (野球), which is made up of the words field, or 野 (ya), and ball, 球 (kyuu).

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Food and Entertainment

In 2013, UNESCO named Japanese food an intangible cultural heritage. The flavors and practices associated with Japanese food are unique. Many of the Japanese loanwords in English reflect that uniqueness. Similarly, many aspects of Japanese entertainment tend to originate in Japan, and the English words borrowed from Japanese show that.

A lot of these loanwords are originally written in kanji, hiragana, or katakana. If you need to review hiragana and katakana, head to this article.

1. Karaoke (カラオケ)

Did you even know this was a Japanese word before Karaoke actually came into contact with Japan or the language? It has roots in the words: kara (空), meaning “empty,” and oke (オケ), meaning “orchestra.” So, together the word actually means orchestraAlso, have you seen anyone do karaoke like the Japanese?

2. Sudoku (すどく)

If you’ve played sudoku and understand it, more power to you. This game and its title originated in Japan in 1984 and have since become very popular worldwide. The su comes from suji or suu (数), meaning number, and the doku (独) means single. The overall aim of the game is to get numbers to appear once in squares in a grid. So literally, the numbers must remain single. Or suuji wa dokushin ni kagiru (数字は独身に限る), which was the original title of the game.

Europeans actually played a similar game in the 18th century. In the 1980s, a Japanese publisher distributed sudoku, which turned into a huge hit and has been popular ever since.

3. Pachinko　(パチンコ)

Hard to spend any time in Japan and not see a pachinko parlor. Pachinko is a kind of pinball game played in arcade games or, more commonly, gambling parlors. Japanese people like to make words that mimic or represent the sound you hear, like the bees buzzing or the snake hissing. The word pachinko is partly made up of a Japanese onomatopoeia. The first part, pachin, is from the sound that the metal pinball makes as it hits an obstacle. The ko is a diminutive suffix that means something like ‘little’.

4. Soy (sauce, beans)

Tofu and miso are obviously Japanese loanwords, but soy? Yes, apparently it comes from しょうゆ (shoyu), which is Japanese for soy sauce. The actual Japanese term for the bean is daizu. Edamame, which are green soybeans, is also commonly used in English.

5. Tamari (たまりしょうゆ)

This one is kind of hip these days. Many recipe bloggers suggest using tamari as a ‘healthy’ alternative to regular soy sauce. Tamari is richer, thicker, and less salty than regular soy sauce, but it is also made from fermented soybeans.

6. Shiitake, maitake, matsutake, and enoki mushrooms (椎茸、舞茸、松茸、えのき)

Did I miss any? Many Japanese mushroom names have been carried over and used as-is in English. The most popular of these might be shiitake, which is often pronounced without the second ‘i’, resulting in shitake.

7. Umami (旨味)

Umami is probably one of the most popular Japanese loanwords in English, being used all the time to describe a distinct savory flavor. This term is a relatively recent adoption into the English language, and it’s somewhat new to Japanese as well.

The word was first coined in 1908 when a Japanese scientist used the word to describe the “5th taste,” which is savoriness. In both Japanese and English, umami generally describes the savory flavor you would find in cooked meats, soy sauce, and mushrooms.

8. Dashi　(だし)

No mention of washoku can exclude dashi, stock made from fish or kelp that is used as the base for many Japanese dishes. Dashi is commonly used in English to mean the same thing.

9. Katsu (curry or chicken katsu)　(かつ)

Katsu refers to cutlets of meat that are breaded using panko and deep-fried. The cutlets are usually pork or chicken. Katsu is served with a sauce or with curry. In fact, in some places overseas, katsu curry has become so popular that the term is used to mean all Japanese curry.

10. Panko　(パン粉)

You might have guessed this from the previous entry, but panko is breadcrumbs. They are commonly used in Japanese cooking and the product and the name have crossed over into English-speaking cultures.

The word panko is actually a combination of a loanword that didn’t come from English and the original Japanese word. “Pan” came from the Portuguese language, pao, and ko (粉) is a Japanese word that means “flour” or “dust”.

The biggest difference between panko and standard breadcrumbs is that panko is made from bread without crusts. Panko’s crustless white bread is coarsely ground into airy, large flakes that give fried foods a light, crunchy coating.

11. Amazake (甘酒)

Making the list of words of Japanese origin recently recorded in the Oxford English Dictionary, amazake is a sweet, fermented drink made from rice. Unlike sake, which is also made from rice, amazake is not alcoholic. It literally means sweet (ama) sake.

12. Manga (漫画)

These loanwords are used the same way in English as they are in Japanese. One distinction is that while manga means comics in general in Japan, the term typically means Japanese comics in English.

13. Anime (アニメ)

Probably the most popular loanword used all the time in English is アニメ (anime), which ironically comes from the word “animation” borrowed from English. But in English, “anime” specifically refers to Japanese animation even though in Japanese it refers to all animation. This term is a great example of words being traded back and forth between two languages.

14. Emoji　(絵文字)

Texting and instant messaging is just not the same without emoji, graphics that help express an emotion when words are just not enough. But the cute, yellow pictogram you’ve been using on your iPhone? The word came from the Japanese language. The kanji 絵 (え) means “picture” and 文字 (もじ) means “character” or “letter.” You might learn some new emoji from the Emojipedia online.

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Sport and Martial Arts

Japanese martial arts are known the world over by their Japanese names. These are quite established loanwords, and the sports themselves continue to gain devotees.

15. Judo　(柔道)

Japanese martial arts are well-known throughout the English-speaking world, by their Japanese names. Judo, a defensive martial art, is no exception. The term originates from soft, gentle (柔; juu) and way, road (道; do). Judo is an Olympic event, and practitioners are usually called judoka (柔道家).

When you’re saying the word “judo” in Japanese, remember to elongate the first syllable: Ju-u-dou. In English, however, you can shorten it.

16. Jujutsu　(柔術)

Precursor to judo, this is also a Japanese unarmed martial art. The first part of the term, juu means gentle, just like in judo and the jutsu (術) means skill or art. There are variant spellings in English, including jiu-jitsu or ju-jitsu. It is also the origin of the name of the famous martial art, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu.

However, historical evidence shows that Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu (BJJ) comes from Judo, but at the time Judo was still being called “Ju-Jutsu,” which is why BJJ has its name today rather than “Brazilian Judo.”

17. Karate　(空手)

Karate is definitely one of those Japanese loanwords that almost feels like it’s always been in English. The term originates from empty (kara) and hand (te), meaning fighting with bare hands. But the history actually gets more interesting.

Karate originates with the indigenous people of Okinawa, who referred to their martial arts as 手(te or tii in Okinawan). But because the Okinawans traded so much with China, Chinese martial arts heavily influenced Karate, so it was initially called “Chinese hand” (唐手), pronounced the same as we know it today. Eventually, after Japan took over Okinawa, the name was changed to 空手 (karate).

18. Kendo　(剣道)

Another Japanese martial art that was simply imported into English, it consists of participants using bamboo swords and wearing protective gear based loosely on samurai armor. Ken means “sword” and do means “way.”

19. Sumo　(相撲)

Often suffixed with ‘wrestling’ in English, sumo means to fight. It’s not just the word that has crossed borders. Many non-Japanese people have succeeded as sumo wrestlers, in what is perceived to be a closed and very traditional world. Check out this quick guide to sumo related terms to learn a bit more about the sport.

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Performing and Literary Arts

From the theater to the page, traditional Japanese performing and literary arts have become well-known in English-speaking cultures.

20. Kabuki　(歌舞伎)

This is a kind of Japanese theater. The Online Etymology Dictionary cites two possible origins of this Japanese loanword. One is that kabuki comes from the verb kabuku, meaning to deviate. The first kabuki performance was given in a shrine by a girl, dressed as a man, which was outside of the norm. The other explanation is that kabuki means ‘art of song and dance,’ from ka (song), bu (dance), and ki (art, skill).

21. Noh　(能)

In Noh theater, performers sing and dance while wearing masks. This loanword comes from the Japanese meaning ‘talent’.

22. Tanka　(短歌)

A poem written using just five lines, tanka means short (tan) song (ka). In English, the poems typically use five lines and 31 syllables, but in Japanese, they are typically written in three lines.

23. Haiku (俳句)

If you’ve heard about haiku, you probably have the impression that it takes immense skill to craft them. These poems are written using a set number of syllables. The haiku consists of three lines, with five syllables in the first line, seven in the second, and five in the third.

Though haiku were originally written in Japanese, English poems following this pattern also go by the same name. Literally meaning light (haikai no) verse (ku), these poems are often about nature.

23. Senryu (川柳)

Senryu is a loanword that refers to another type of Japanese poetry that’s similar to haiku. It tends to talk about people, rather than nature. This form was named after a poet who frequently practiced it.

Other Japanese Loanwords We Use in English

From business to bedding and natural disasters, Japanese loanwords are used in many areas of life. The following words don’t fall neatly into the categories we have here. But they are still commonly used.

25. Tycoon (大君)

You’ve probably heard this word used a lot with another t-word, tech, as in tech tycoon. Its origins have little do with technology, however. Taikun was the name foreigners gave to the shogun (another loanword) when they came to Japan in the 1800s. Over time, taikun (great lord) became tycoon. Today, the word refers to someone of tremendous wealth and power.

26. Honcho　(班長)

This is another loanword often used alliteratively with head, as in head honcho, meaning leader. The term originates from Japanese han (group) and cho (leader), and was apparently picked up by foreigners in Japan during the second world war.

27. Skosh (少し: Sukoshi)

Have you ever noticed someone saying, “Just a skosh.” Maybe you’re asking if you need to add more salt when you are making soup. This loanword is a shortening of the Japanese sukoshi, meaning a little. It was adopted by the US servicemen when they were stationed in Japan after World War II. It is used in the same way in English and carries the nuance of a really tiny amount.

28. Zen　(善)

This loanword originates from the Japanese school of Zen Buddhism that focuses on meditation. In common use in English, zen means calm and peaceful, and doesn’t explicitly refer to Buddhism.

29. Futon　(布団)

Futon is one of those loanwords that perhaps many people have forgotten is, in fact, a loanword. It’s used to describe a flat mattress that can be rolled up, which is traditional bedding in Japan. However, in English, people refer to couches that have pull-out beds as futons. The fu in this loanword means sheet or cloth, and the ton means group.

30. Ikigai (生きがい)

Ikigai, as a concept, has been making waves in the English-speaking world in recent years. Iki means life and gai means value, so the term translates to ‘reason for being’. The idea is that with a reason for being or a purpose, people can live more fulfilling lives, as those lives get longer.

31. Tsunami (津波)

Originating from harbor (tsu) and wave (nami), this word has been in use in many unfortunate circumstances recently. As with the original Japanese, it describes a large sea wave caused by an earthquake. Tsunami has also been used in a figurative sense to mean a large and sudden amount of something.

32. Samurai (侍)

Many words from Japanese history are usually adopted directly into English, and samurai is no exception. Samurai describes a specific warrior class that only existed in the context of Japan. Calling them “Japanese knights” just wouldn’t capture what they were and the place they had in Japanese society.

Likewise, many other historical Japanese terms for different social positions or figures, like shogun, daimyo, or even ninja, are simply borrowed in English.

33. Katana (刀)

While katana actually just means “sword,” in English it has come to refer to the specific Japanese sword with its characteristic curved blade that was used by the samurai. Likely due to its unique aesthetics, carefully crafted by skilled blacksmiths, it caught the attention of foreigners. Thus, now we use the word katana to describe the iconic sword from Japan.

The kimono is a beautiful, elegant garment that has come to be known as the national dress of Japan. So, there’s no question why English adopted the word kimono to describe this iconic piece of clothing. There isn’t even an equivalent type of clothing to the kimono in English-speaking countries; while there are dresses and robes, none of them are quite a kimono.

While English has the word “bullet train,” it’s not uncommon for people to opt to use the word “shinkansen” instead. Often when people visit Japan, they might say they want to ride the “shinkansen” rather than the “bullet train.”

The truth is, languages constantly borrow from each other, showing how we exchange ideas all the time.

items.author: Wakaba Oto
